papers.title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.

papers.title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
papers.abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per-query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO-Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

papers.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
papers.metadata: Title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents Jingwei Song, Zhisheng Chen, Bingfan Zeng, Jing Tang, Yubo Hou, Jinhao Jing, Zhengwei Xie, Linfeng Zhang Comments: 39 pages, 6 figures Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. papers.title: Mapless, Stabilizing, and Anti-Stuck Flipper Control for Articulated Tracked Robots

papers.title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.

papers.title: Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
papers.abstract: Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. However, these methods assume static scenes, limiting realism in the presence of dynamic phenomena ubiquitous in real-world environments. While coherent motion (e.g., humans or vehicles) can be captured and reconstructed, high-frequency effects such as flowing water remain intractable under casual capture conditions, where dense multi-view, high-speed acquisition is not feasible. We present a method to animate water in static 3DGS scenes, enabling visually plausible motion without requiring dynamic capture or physical simulation. Our approach estimates 2D optical flow from reference images or model renderings and lifts it into a consistent 3D Eulerian motion field. We propose a cinemagraph-inspired algorithm that applies this motion field to deform Gaussian primitives, producing temporally seamless looping animations. The resulting representation retains real-time rendering performance, significantly enhances perceptual realism, and preserves free-viewpoint navigation within the scene. We evaluate our method on a newly captured dataset of in-the-wild waterfall scenes and demonstrate clear improvements over prior work in dynamic Gaussian splatting and 3D cinemagraph generation in visual quality and computational efficiency.

papers.title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation
papers.abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. BT-Agent's largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.

papers.title: Beyond the Snowflakes: Disentangling Weather Effects from Confounding Meta-Factors in LiDAR Object Detection
papers.abstract: Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) is critical for autonomous perception, yet its performance is known to degrade in adverse weather. While existing literature models snow as atmospheric noise that degrades performance, our granular evaluation on the WADS-3D and CADC datasets reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: detection accuracy consistently improves as snow intensity increases. Through ablation study and meta-information analysis, we reconcile this by confirming that while falling snow acts as noise, its negative impact is outweighed by a dominant, concurrent factor: significantly increased object point count. We hypothesize that this object point count boost acts as a geometric enhancement, driven by snow accumulation increasing vehicle surface area and a shift from specular to diffuse reflectance. Our findings demonstrate that evaluating perception systems using broad weather-severity bins without accounting for correlated object-level data can lead to misleading conclusions about detector robustness. We conclude that accurate evaluation requires decoupling atmospheric noise from surface accumulation effects and outline future research to validate these physical models. The WADS-3D dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/wads-3d/.

papers.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.

papers.metadata: Title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song Comments: Project website: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.

papers.title: Splat2Act: From Captured Scenes to Personalized VLA Manipulation
papers.abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.

papers.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. papers.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
papers.metadata: Title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures Yuming Fu, Weijia Wu, Jing Chen, Jiahao Tang, Feifei Chen, Hongyu Zhu, Xin Jin, Alex Jinpeng Wang Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.

papers.title: OIL: An Object Interaction Layer for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
papers.metadata: Title: OIL: An Object Interaction Layer for Humanoid Whole-Body Control Pranay Dugar, Mohitvishnu S. Gadde, Rajesh Mangannavar, Aayam Kumar Shrestha, Alan Fern Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: Recent progress in learned whole-body controllers for humanoid robots has enabled robust free-space motion by tracking kinematic targets such as joint or end-effector trajectories. This interface provides a useful abstraction for upstream systems, including motion capture, teleoperation, or generative models, which can specify desired motion without reasoning about forces or balance. However, this abstraction has largely been limited to robot motion, requiring task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction. We introduce OIL, an Object Interaction Layer that extends the kinematic command interface of whole-body control to include desired object motion and contact. OIL augments a standard controller with object-centric commands and translates them into coordinated whole-body behavior while preserving locomotion and balance. This design enables a single learned policy to execute non-prehensile interactions, including pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport, directly from object-level kinematic targets without task-specific retraining. In simulation, we demonstrate that object-level commands improve performance over robot-centric controllers while matching task-specific policies across variations in object properties such as mass and size. We further demonstrate zero-shot generalization to novel behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid robot.

papers.title: Building Trustworthy Household Robots through Open-World Safety
papers.abstract: Foundation models are expanding robot capabilities, enabling robots to handle more diverse objects, follow sophisticated instructions, and operate in complex environments. These advances bring us to a future in which robots become part of everyday household life. However, cluttered, dynamic household environments also expose robots to unfamiliar objects, tasks, and interactions, making reliable zero-shot task completion an ongoing challenge for robotics research. From a security perspective, we argue for open-world safety: household robots should preserve specified safety requirements in unseen situations, including when they cannot complete the requested task. Safety protections must account for context and interactions that persist across actions and tasks. In this position paper, we examine why existing safety methods can fail to provide this protection. Protection can fail through misinterpreted context, overlooked past interactions, or stopping and recovery strategies that become unsafe under unfamiliar conditions. We therefore propose a research agenda to specify, learn, and ground safety requirements, enforce them with reliable recovery, and evaluate the generalization of such protections. We call for household robots whose safety protections remain reliable beyond the situations, context, and history used to train and develop them, to achieve open-world safety.

papers.title: Residual Compliant Policy: Learning Compliant Policies from Few Demonstrations
papers.metadata: Title: Residual Compliant Policy: Learning Compliant Policies from Few Demonstrations Chunyu Jiang, Yichen Cai, Shuai Li, Wenbin Sun, João Carvalho, Kostas Daniilidis, Oleg Arenz, Cristiana de Farias, Jan Peters Comments: 9 pages, 6 figures. Project website: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to be precise in free space to establish the intended contacts, and compliant once in contact to avoid excessive forces. Imitation learning has proven effective for simpler manipulation tasks, but the compliance underlying a demonstration is not directly observable and is therefore difficult to infer from demonstration data alone. We present a framework that makes compliance explicit at every stage. During data collection, the operator teleoperates the real robot while a synchronized digital twin visualizes the error between the commanded reference and the achieved pose, making the current compliance visible, and selects between two discrete compliance modes. To generalize across object poses, we combine Laplacian editing, which retargets trajectories efficiently but is not physics-consistent during contact, with simulation-based trajectory optimization, which enforces physical plausibility but offers no manual guidance. Finally, a residual reinforcement learning policy refines the interaction forces by adjusting the reference pose of the underlying admittance controller. We evaluate on three flipping and pushing tasks on a Franka FR3 based on a total of 7 demonstrations across tasks. Our method is successful on all 40 out-of-distribution trials, compared to 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines, with our base policy alone reaching 35/40.

papers.metadata: Title: From bits to atoms: A survey of cross-layer safety in Embodied AI Tuo Feng, Yue Zhang, Shiji Zhou, Zhaoxin Fan, Wenguan Wang, Xiaowei Chi, Tianyu Shen, Xiangtai Li, Xuesong Bai, Zheng Zhu, Sirui Han, Boyu Zhou, Zhaosong Wang, Shizhe Chen, Zilong Zheng, Chenjia Bai, Jiangmiao Pang, Yaodong Yang, Hao Zhao, Di Hu, Li Yi, Yan Huang, Qi Wu, Hanwang Zhang, Fei Gao, Shanghang Zhang, Hongsheng Li, Jianye Hao, Yuan Zhang, Yingjie Xia, Jian Shen, Cewu Lu, Hui Zhang, Kai Chen, Wenwu Yu, Badong Chen, Jungong Han, Yike Guo Comments: Review article published in AI Plus. 25 pages, 6 figures. papers.abstract: Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces cyber-physical risks because digital failures and attacks can cause physical harm. This survey organizes embodied AI safety through a four-layer reference architecture -- comprising the physical interaction, system and middleware, algorithm and decision, and cloud-edge and data layers -- and uses it to connect vulnerabilities, propagation paths, and safeguards across the system stack. Furthermore, the survey systematizes composite attack chains, outlines multi-layered defense strategies, and reviews representative embodied safety benchmarks. Ultimately, we advocate for unifying software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints to build trustworthy systems capable of operating safely within human-centric environments.

papers.title: RAIN: Robotic Task Generalization with Region-Aware Interaction Networks
papers.metadata: Title: RAIN: Robotic Task Generalization with Region-Aware Interaction Networks Seunghun Lee, Kyuhwan Shim, Yeogyeong Song, Seung Hwan Kim, Sihaeng Lee, Byoung-Tak Zhang, Sunghoon Im, Gunhee Lee Comments: Project page: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{Region-Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN)}, which formulates a task as a sequence of goal-conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target-region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target-adaptive Cross-View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target-directed trajectories and actions. A Transition Head estimates subtask completion to enable automatic transitions. We also introduce a \textbf{Reference-based Retargeting Strategy (RRS)}, which uses recorded trajectories to synthesize smooth approaches to reference interactions with alternative target regions, without collecting additional data. Experiments on \textbf{LIBERO-Analogy}, our new benchmark for robotic task generalization, and real-world tabletop tasks demonstrate that RAIN generalizes more robustly than existing VLA baselines.

papers.title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning from Real-Robot Interaction without High-Quality State Estimates
papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.

papers.title: Refuses in Chat, Complies with Arms: LLM Refusal Does Not Survive Robot Control
papers.metadata: Title: Refuses in Chat, Complies with Arms: LLM Refusal Does Not Survive Robot Control Edward Sun, Christopher Leet, Sravanthi Machcha, Achyutha Menon, Tzu Kit Chan, Yuchen Cui, Jay Chooi Comments: 7 pages Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.

papers.title: Terrain Traversal Without Motion Priors: Expert-Routed Humanoid Locomotion at Deployment Fidelity
papers.metadata: Title: Terrain Traversal Without Motion Priors: Expert-Routed Humanoid Locomotion at Deployment Fidelity Thanh Ly, Chien Le, Truong-Duy Dang, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Duy-Dung Le, Vien Anh Ngo, An T. Le Comments: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five-expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model-based planner, refined by six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception-to-actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment-fidelity simulator, it crosses an $85$\,m five-segment waypoint course $18$ of $20$ times end-to-end ($90\%$, Wilson $95\%$ CI $70$--$97$) and succeeds $20/20$ on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches $0\%$ on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves $72.4\%$ of foot placements across at least one grid-cell boundary, which produces real sub-grid correction. We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label-free routers collapse to near-uniform activation, and a self-supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.

papers.title: Do My Samples Help? Compute Budget Allocation for Real-World Sampling-Based MPC in Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.

papers.title: From Hitter to Player: Separating Motor Execution and Strategy in Competitive Humanoid Table Tennis
papers.metadata: Title: From Hitter to Player: Separating Motor Execution and Strategy in Competitive Humanoid Table Tennis Fanrong Dong, Ziyi Sun, Ziqi Han, Junhan Sun, Lei Ye, Zetong Jing, Hao Zhao, Shaoxun Liu, Rongrong Wang Comments: 8 pages, 7 figures. papers.abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. papers.title: An Explicit Bound for the First Dirichlet Eigenvalue via Two Moments
papers.abstract: Let $(M^n,g)$, $n\ge2$, be a compact connected Riemannian manifold with smooth nonempty boundary, $\operatorname{Ric}_M\ge(n-1)Kg$ for $K>0$, and nonnegative outward boundary mean curvature. We derive an explicit algebraic lower bound $B_η$ for the first Dirichlet eigenvalue from Kasue's mixed inradius model. With $R$ the inradius and $s=4KR^2/π^2$, the bound involves one square root and approximates the model eigenvalue with relative error $O_n(s^4)$ as $s\downarrow0$ for fixed $n$. The construction uses the first two moments of a positive representation of the averaged model potential and a sharp pointwise corrector estimate. For the chosen spectral transfer, the first two moments determine an optimal bound. We also show that the model eigenvalue is the geometric infimum at fixed $(n,K,R)$. For $0<s<1$, it is approached by smooth collapsing balls with sectional curvature at least $K$ and totally geodesic boundary. At the maximal inradius, the model value is attained by the round hemisphere. The bound strictly improves the variance refinement throughout $0<s\le1$. We also give a direct algebraic comparison with an optimized power-test benchmark.

papers.title: Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.

papers.title: Prelocality No-Go Theorems and Exactly Solvable Relational History Hamiltonians
papers.abstract: Exact permutation covariance does not itself supply a sparse metric geometry. For permutation-covariant, full-support $k$-body interaction orbits, the incident interaction norm scales as $\binom{N-1}{k-1}|J_N|\|h\|$; such orbits cannot have uniformly finite range in metrics of diverging diameter. A permutation-invariant Hamiltonian diagonal in the graph basis has ground-state multiplicity at least $N!/|\mathrm{Aut}(G)|$ whenever $G$ is a ground graph. We give a quantitative version for approximately symmetric energies, together with fixed-radius connectivity and unitary-isometry obstructions. The trace-distance asymmetry of an arbitrary state also bounds its probability of selecting one labeled graph. We then construct two exactly solvable finite relational history Hamiltonians. A cyclic clock with a reversible incidence update has a unique ground state; gauge reduction yields a cycle Laplacian with a rank-one pin and the exact gap $Δ_{N,L}=E_* (1-\cosθ_L)$, where $\tan(Lθ_L/2)=1/\sinθ_L$ and $0<θ_L<π/L$. In particular, $Δ_{N,L}/E_*=π^2/(2L^2)-2π^2/L^3+O(L^{-4})$, independently of the number of vertices. In an alternative order-free architecture, one clock qubit per unordered pair gives commuting four-local terms, $2^N$ ground states and a size-independent gap $E_*(1-1/\sqrt2)$. A fixed-weight control penalty selects $\binom Nq$ ground states without reducing the gap. These exact finite results expose clock and locality resource tradeoffs; they do not establish an emergent geometric phase.

papers.title: SenseWeather: Multimodal Sensing for Robust Robotic Perception under Extreme Conditions
papers.abstract: Robotic perception must remain reliable when extreme environmental conditions severely degrade the primary RGB observation. Although robotic platforms commonly carry complementary sensors such as depth and infrared, much of the modern perception stack remains RGB-centric, creating a mismatch between multimodal onboard sensing and pretrained downstream models. We study whether complementary sensing can be used upstream to recover a task-compatible RGB observation that preserves existing perception capabilities without modifying or retraining the downstream stack. To this end, we introduce SenseWeather, a controlled multimodal benchmark for robotic perception under severe rain, snow, dust, fog, and darkness, with registered RGB, depth, and infrared observations, clean references, and grounded high-level perception tasks. We further develop Fusion-to-RGB, with two parameter-efficient sensor-fusion realizations based on token-space fusion for a diffusion transformer and residual latent conditioning for an inpainting UNet. Across frozen open-vocabulary grounding and vision-language models, RGB+D+IR fusion improves all paired downstream comparisons over the corresponding RGB-only restorers, including AP50 gains across all ten detector comparisons. Importantly, these perception gains do not consistently follow conventional image-fidelity metrics, and increasing weather severity does not induce monotonic downstream degradation. These results show that complementary sensing can preserve reusable robotic perception under extreme conditions, while highlighting task-level perception robustness as an objective distinct from visual restoration quality.

papers.title: When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
papers.abstract: Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting

papers.title: Digraph Laplacian spectra: Counterexamples to the 2005 polygon conjecture
papers.abstract: Let $Λ_n$ be the set of all eigenvalues of standardized Laplacian matrices of order $n$. In 2005, a polygon $S_n\subseteqΛ_n$ was constructed, and it was conjectured that $Λ_n=S_n$. We observe that $S_n$ is a zonotope, which gives a short proof of $S_n\subseteqΛ_n$, and we describe $Λ_n$ as a union, over all vectors $v$, of intersections of zonotopes $Z_i(v)$ built from the ratios $v_j/v_i$. For a vector whose components are the $n$ distinct $n$th roots of unity, every $Z_i(v)$ equals $S_n$. We then show that the conjecture is false for $n=7$: the directed $6$-cycle with one vertex duplicated has an eigenvalue lying $2.1\cdot10^{-4}$ beyond one edge of $S_7$. For the analogous digraph of order $n$, the corresponding eigenvalue lies at signed distance $δ_n\sim\frac{π^2}{2n^4}$ beyond the supporting line of the analogous edge of $S_n$, so the construction yields counterexamples for all sufficiently large $n$; numerically, it does so for every $7\le n\le300$. We also prove that $S_m\subseteq S_n$ whenever $m\mid n$, with $S_m\setminus\{0,1\}$ lying in the interior of $S_n$ for $n\ge3m$.

papers.title: Embodied Zero-Shot Task Planning via Hardware-Aware LLM-VLM Integration for Grounded Robotic Manipulation
papers.metadata: Title: Embodied Zero-Shot Task Planning via Hardware-Aware LLM-VLM Integration for Grounded Robotic Manipulation Lonnie Tankersley, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Soroush Korivand Comments: 6 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted and presented at the 25th IEEE International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications (ICMLA 2026), Oct 5-7, 2026 Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.

papers.title: Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages
papers.abstract: Calibrated typed-decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre-registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya-multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence-gated cascade that sends Jev's 10-30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4-14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre-registration, code and all predictions.

papers.title: Make π0.5 Learn to Call Astra for Reliable Robot Manipulation
papers.metadata: Title: Make π0.5 Learn to Call Astra for Reliable Robot Manipulation Jianli Sun, Chengxiang Li, Yonglin Tian Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $π_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $π_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. papers.title: Refine Where It Matters: Contact-Adaptive Meshing for Deformable Object Manipulation
papers.metadata: Title: Refine Where It Matters: Contact-Adaptive Meshing for Deformable Object Manipulation Gabriel Johnson, Tom Olesch, Fei Liu Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: Deformable-object manipulation requires accurate modeling of highly localized contact while maintaining simulation speeds suitable for interactive use. Uniformly fine tetrahedral meshes can resolve these interactions, but they introduce unnecessary degrees of freedom throughout the object. Coarse meshes are more efficient, yet they may under-resolve contact-induced deformation. We present a contact-adaptive mesh refinement framework that introduces spatial resolution only where it is most useful. The method uses geometric, elastic, and contact quantities already available from the deformable-body solver to score candidate edges. A fully GPU-parallel procedure then selects a conflict-free subset and updates both mesh topology and physical state directly within the simulation loop. We evaluate the approach on real deformable-object manipulation sequences. Adaptive refinement reduces simulation-to-real error, improves agreement with a fine-mesh reference, and remains substantially more efficient than uniformly fine simulation. These results show that local refinement can improve physical fidelity without incurring the cost of a globally fine discretization. The framework provides a practical basis for contact-rich simulation in interactive manipulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.

papers.title: Axiom-0: Hierarchical Self-Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies
papers.metadata: Title: Axiom-0: Hierarchical Self-Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies Renbin Shu, Jing Yang, Xiangyuan You, Guolin Qiu, Yufei Xia, Yiming Zhu, Nanjun Dai, Fei Zhang, Feng Wu, Keke Tang Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

papers.title: Branching fraction measurement of the $B^0\to K^+π^-μ^+μ^-$ decay at high dihadron mass
papers.abstract: This Letter presents the first measurement of the $B^{0} \to K^{+}π^{-}μ^{+}μ^{-}$ differential branching fraction in the region of the dihadron $K^+π^-$ mass, $m_{Kπ}$, $1000< m_{Kπ} < 1835\,\text{MeV}/c^{2}$. This decay mode is mediated by the quark-level transition $b \to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}$, for which the measured effective couplings show tensions with Standard Model predictions. The analysis is performed using proton-proton collision data collected with the LHCb detector between 2011 and 2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $8.4\,\text{fb}^{-1}$. The differential branching fraction is determined across different regions of dimuon mass squared, $q^2$, in the interval $0.1 < q^2 < 18.0\,\text{GeV}^2/c^{4}$, as well as in different regions of $ m_{Kπ}$ in the interval $1.1 < q^2 < 6.0\,\text{GeV}^2/c^{4}$. The results represent the first differential measurement of the branching fraction across $m_{Kπ}$ within the selected dihadron-mass region, and the first observation of the decay within this region above the $J/ψ$ resonance.

papers.title: Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling
papers.metadata: Title: Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling Dayou Li, Jionghao Wang, Peihao Wang, Jiuzhou Lei, Hao Wang, Jichen Chai, Hezhen Hu, Minghui Zheng, Zhangyang Wang, Xin Li, Wenping Wang, Zhiwen Fan Comments: Project page: this https URL Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Reward design remains a major bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation. Handcrafted dense rewards can compensate for the limited guidance provided by sparse rewards, but require substantial task-specific reward engineering. Learning rewards from videos provides a scalable, data-driven alternative to manual reward design. However, existing video-based rewards are often computed in entangled visual spaces where task-relevant state changes are confounded with extraneous visual variation. As a result, the learned reward may respond to visual distractors instead of actual task execution. To address this limitation, we propose DiTaR (Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling), a framework for learning dense rewards from heterogeneous videos. DiTaR learns a continuous task-relevant representation from multi-frame video latents through an asymmetric two-stage procedure that suppresses task-irrelevant visual variation. In the task-relevant latent space, we train a history- and language-conditioned rectified-flow model to capture task dynamics and derive a directional dense reward from temporal changes in dynamics compatibility. Together, these components enable reward modeling directly over task-relevant dynamics rather than generic visual variation. DiTaR substantially improves policy learning on MetaWorld-v3 and ManiSkill over video-based reward baselines, and transfers to real-world offline RL through reward relabeling. Reward analyses further show that DiTaR provides more reliable rewards.

papers.title: Solutions of Roy equations for variable pion mass
papers.abstract: The Roy equations for the $S$ and $P$ waves are solved for pion masses below the physical value in the region between threshold and $s_A=0.84\GeV^2$. The analysis is based on the assumption that the phenomenological input above $s_A$ can be used essentially unchanged. Moreover, for $M_π\le M_{π,\mathrm{phys}}$, the chiral perturbation theory predictions for the two $S$-wave scattering lengths provide a very reliable additional input to the Roy equations. The outcome is an accurate description of the $S$ and $P$ partial waves as the light-quark masses decrease towards the chiral limit. As a test of the approach, we evaluate the first few threshold parameters of the $S$, $P$, and $D$ waves via Wanders' sum rules and find excellent agreement with chiral perturbation theory across the entire range $0 \le M_π\le M_{π,\mathrm{phys}}$. We further solve the Roy equations for pion masses above the physical value (up to $240\MeV$) and show that the resulting solutions agree well with existing lattice data at $M_π=239\MeV$. The present work paves the way for analyses of lattice data that fully incorporate the constraints of analyticity, unitarity, and crossing symmetry, and provides the basis for an accurate study of the dependence of the $σ$ and $ρ$ resonances on the light-quark masses, both of which will be addressed in future work.

papers.title: Semiclassical state on algebra of observables for de Sitter space and time reversal symmetry
papers.abstract: In de Sitter static patch holography, coupling bulk quantum fields to an observer's dynamical clock yields a type II$_1$ von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}_+$ of gauge-invariant observables. However, the unique tracial state on this algebra fails to reproduce semiclassical bulk correlation functions. We resolve this issue by introducing a family of heavy-clock states, representing an observer reference frame with heavy inertia. We prove that in the heavy-clock limit, $n$-point correlation functions of gauge-invariant dressed observables reproduce the bulk quantum field correlation functions on de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we investigate a generalized observer Hamiltonian $\widehat{H}_{\rm obs}=|\widehatπ|$ that incorporates both forward-running ($π\geq 0$) and backward-running ($π<0$) clocks. The resulting von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ of gauge-invariant observables remains a type~II$_1$ factor and is isomorphic to $\mathcal{M}_+\otimes M_2(\mathbb{C})$, where $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ is the algebra of $2\times2$ complex matrices transforming between the two clock orientations. Time-reversal symmetry is implemented in this setting as an anti-unitary operator that exchanges the two clock orientations, yielding a type~II$_1$ von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{F}$ of gauge-invariant, time-reversal-invariant observables. We generalize the heavy-clock state construction to both $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{F}$, showing that $n$-point correlation functions calculated in heavy-clock states match the corresponding semiclassical bulk correlation functions. Finally, by coupling Einstein gravity to the Brown--Kuchař dust field, we derive the observer Hamiltonian $\widehat{H}_{\rm obs}=|\widehatπ|$ from a perturbative reduction along the observer's worldline in the $G \to 0$ limit. This provides a field-theoretic foundation for the observer model developed in this work.

papers.title: Visualizing the World Model in an Agent's Value Function

papers.title: Observation-Referenced Tissue Deformation Forecasting with Tool-Driven and Residual Dynamics
papers.abstract: Forecasting tissue deformation from future instrument motion could support predictive planning and increasingly autonomous surgical systems. We study this problem using a scene-specific differentiable surface model fitted to an observed tool-tissue interaction window. Rather than forecasting absolute simulated positions, we introduce an \textit{observation-referenced} formulation that anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation and adds only the deformation induced by the known, preplanned future tool trajectory. This reduces sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets while preserving the predicted deformation response. The physical model uses differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics with scene-specific rigidity, attachment, region scale, and grasp coupling. We further introduce an optional \textit{observation-referenced residual model} combining graph-spectral spatial modes with periodic harmonic dynamics for structured motion not explained by the tool input. We evaluate the framework retrospectively on 12 surgical manipulation clips from three datasets. Observation referencing provides the largest gain, with a median within-clip error ratio of $0.598$ relative to the corresponding absolute simulation forecast. The optional periodic residual further improves forecasting when the remaining motion exhibits periodic structure. These results support observation-referenced deformation prediction as a practical building block for future surgical world models, digital twins, and generative simulators that must predict how tissue evolves under instrument actions.

papers.title: An Abresch-Rosenberg type tensor and a gap theorem for CMC hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{S}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{H}^n\times\mathbb{R}$

An exact integrated Simons identity yields explicit gap theorems, valid for every $h>1$ in $\mathbb{H}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ and every $h>(n\int_0^{π/2}\sin^{n-1}r\,dr)^{-1}$ in $\mathbb{S}^n\times\mathbb{R}$. We compare the pinching thresholds with the pointwise algebraic level that implies convexity. In $\mathbb{H}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ the explicit pinching conditions imply strict convexity, so there the method gives an independent proof with explicit constants. In $\mathbb{S}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ the pinching region exceeds the convexity level for $n\in\{3,4\}$ and every admissible $h$, and for $n\geq5$ whenever $h^2\geq n/(6(n+2))$; there the gap theorem does not require convexity to be known in advance. We also determine second-order large-$h$ asymptotics of the thresholds.

papers.title: Latent World Action Model for GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Pixel-space world models have recently emerged as a promising approach for GUI agents, predicting future screens prior to execution and subsequently re-perceiving them for action selection. However, this two-stage paradigm faces two key challenges in GUI environments: (L1) the high computational cost of pixel reconstruction and (L2) the need to reconstruct large and diverse appearance-level details beyond what is required for action selection. In practice, this screen-generation objective can induce an identity shortcut problem, where future-state prediction largely preserves the current state rather than capturing action-induced changes. In this work, we reformulate GUI world modeling by shifting the prediction target from full-screen reconstruction to action-induced future information in latent space. Concretely, we leverage a large multimodal model as the latent world model, whose shared representations support two dedicated heads for both action selection and predictive transition modeling. The action head directly translates these latent representations into action selection, while the transition head captures action-conditioned future information. To mitigate the identity shortcut, we further introduce an action-aware contrastive objective that encourages the transition representations to capture discriminative action-induced changes. Extensive experiments across offline and online GUI settings show that our method achieves up to 31.9% and 40.6% relative gains in success rate over pixel-space world models, respectively, while substantially reducing inference latency by up to 98.9%. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/latent2world.

papers.title: Mapping Tire-Road Friction Coefficients Along Driven Trajectories
papers.abstract: Information of the tire-road friction coefficient is critical for intelligent vehicle systems, as friction establishes the limits at which the vehicle can be manoeuvred without loss of control. While there is extensive literature on online friction estimation, no previous studies have explored post-processing and mapping friction coefficients along a driven trajectory based on recorded sensor data. Mapped friction information could be shared by connected vehicles, enabling proactive measures in low-friction areas. This paper presents an offline post-processing method, FrictionMap, for mapping friction coefficients from recorded driving data. The method operates on commonly available on-board vehicle sensor information, and requires only a basic vehicle parameter set and a slip threshold as prior knowledge. FrictionMap runs an extended Kalman filter combined with a Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother to estimate vehicle dynamics. Data points where the friction limit is observable are identified by filtering points based on tire slip. A Gaussian process is fitted to these points to acquire a continuous estimate of the friction coefficient along the trajectory. FrictionMap is validated via a simulation study, and shown to outperform commonly used online friction estimation techniques. The code implementation and the simulation benchmark are released as open-source after paper acceptance to enable further research.

papers.metadata: Title: RoboFake: Are Deepfake Detectors Ready for Humanoid Face Robots? Hao Chen, Junnan Xu Comments: 10 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Robotics (cs.RO)

All thresholds are fixed on FaceForensics++, and every result is compared with real human faces that went through the same processing as the robot videos. At a threshold that flags 5% of real faces, three detectors flag almost every physical robot frame, while two flag fewer than 7%. However, it does not track synthesis: with only the face visible, three of the six detectors give the physical robot a higher fake score than its synthesized video. The response is also fragile, and light JPEG compression is enough to push most robot frames below the threshold for some detectors. Our results suggest that current detectors flag today's robots because their faces do not look human, not because they recognize a forgery. papers.title: GeoFix: Geometry Fixing for 4D Consistent Generation
papers.abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. papers.title: MvFFN: Multi-view Floor plan Feed-forward Network for Unposed Wide-Baseline Panorama Layout Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Reconstructing accurate camera poses and floor-plan layouts from sparse, unposed, wide-baseline RGB panoramas remains a challenging open problem. Direct multi-room floor-plan prediction is especially difficult in this setting: pose, geometry, semantics, and global layout structure are tightly coupled, yet a complete floor-plan is hard to learn as a single global output. Our key insight is to keep the model's predictions strictly local. Multi-view Ordered Wall Instance Segmentation (MOIS) is designed around this concept. Each panorama column predicts only the wall it observes plus the next two adjacent walls in clockwise order. The global wall partition, room layouts, and shared coordinates emerge from deterministic aggregation of overlapping local predictions. A downstream Layout Chaining (LC) post processing pipeline then assembles these predictions into multi-room floor-plans with shared global coordinates, consistent wall identities, and connected room structure. The dense MOIS predictions recover cross-view wall identity and local within-room connectivity more accurately than composed modular baselines, and the assembled layouts substantially outperform prior methods on wall and junction level accuracy. We also introduce the ZInD-CrossView dataset, which augments ZInD with globally unique wall instances and cross-view segmentation labels for this task.

papers.title: Manifold Navigation Learning Using Recurrent Networks: Efficient Training Techniques
papers.abstract: Position tracking is a well-studied problem in Euclidean navigation, yet comparatively little attention has been given to navigation on general manifolds, where motion is governed by the underlying geometry of the space. In this work, we formalize the problem of manifold navigation as a velocity-driven tracking task and propose a coordinate-chart-based learning framework in which learning models operate entirely in a Euclidean representation. Predicted trajectories are mapped to the manifold via an immersion function prior to error computation, allowing geometric consistency to be evaluated without explicitly enforcing manifold constraints during learning. Within this framework, we focus on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) for sequential position prediction on curved manifolds after comparisons with alternative recurrent architectures. We evaluate our GRU models, trained with pertinent custom loss functions, against both a standard MSE loss function and a naive vector-addition baseline. We evaluate our approach on both analytically (and numerically) defined manifolds, as well as a surface reconstructed from a LiDAR point cloud. Our results show that recurrent models can learn to approximate manifold-constrained dynamics from velocity sequences and consistently outperform Euclidean baselines. Our results demonstrate that certain custom loss functions significantly improve long-horizon prediction accuracy compared to conventional point-wise loss functions.

papers.title: PILOT: Guiding Long-Horizon World-Model Planning for Robot Manipulation with Visual Subgoals and Policy Priors
papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. papers.metadata: Title: Continuous-Time Cloth Dynamics with Physics-Informed Neural ODEs Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Zhuo He, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: We present ContinuousCloth, a continuous-time, physics-informed neural solver for deformable cloth dynamics that enforces a spring--mass ODE within a neural trajectory model. papers.title: Learning Transferable World-Action Models from Task-Paired Human Videos
papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.

papers.title: Deep learning from a control vantage point
papers.abstract: This article offers an overview of recent developments in deep learning from a control vantage point. It reviews several classes of models including feedforward and residual neural networks, transformers, large-language models, and selective state space models while explaining how control theory plays an important role in understanding their training, properties, or architecture design. The article explains how residual neural networks can be interpreted as the discretization of a continuous-time control system thereby enabling the use of control theoretic techniques for its analysis. To illustrate the power of this bridge between control and deep learning, two technical results are discussed: 1) the ability of a residual neural network to approximate arbitrary continuous functions is a non-standard controllability problem that can be solved using geometric nonlinear control and 2) transformers, the key architectural component of most large language-models, can be seen the discretization of a consensus algorithm and thus large language-models exhibit consensus. Another point of contact between control theory and deep learning is the connection between backpropagation, the algorithm used to train neural networks, and optimal control. The article addresses how the older connection between these problems, established in the 80's using discrete-time models can be reconciled with the more recent approach using continuous-time models. Several open problems and directions for future research are discussed, including selective state-space models, a recent class of models inspired by the models used in control.

papers.title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations
papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.

papers.title: Memory Without Curation: Learning Multi-Stream Latent Memory for Robot Policies
papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. papers.title: Red-Teaming of Vision-Language-Action Models via Quality Diversity Environment Generation
papers.metadata: Title: Red-Teaming of Vision-Language-Action Models via Quality Diversity Environment Generation Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita Comments: 8 pages, 5 figures Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)
papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q-DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine-tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high-failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self-imitation fine-tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q-DEG improves robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine-tuned using data collected from two red-teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q-DEG facilitates sim-to-real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd-env.github.io/qdeg/.

papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
papers.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure. We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.

papers.metadata: Title: Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation Jinjie Li, Yicheng Chen, Haokun Liu, Moju Zhao Comments: 3 pages, 2 figures. papers.abstract: Omnidirectional aerial robots offer full 6-DoF independent control over position and orientation, making them popular for aerial manipulation.
